Epidemiology begins with counting. The hard part is not the arithmetic. It is
knowing what belongs in the denominator, and what that choice means.

## A count is not a measure

> "Kolar reported 480 tuberculosis cases last year; Tumkur reported 210."

You cannot compare those. Kolar might be 3 times the size. A bare count
answers "how much work is there", which matters for planning drugs and beds. It
does not answer "how bad is it here", which needs a denominator.

Every measure below is a count divided by something. Which something you choose
is the lesson.

## Prevalence — how many have it now

$$\text{Prevalence} = \frac{\text{people with the disease at a point in time}}{\text{people in the population at that time}}$$

Prevalence is a **proportion**. It has no units and it sits between 0 and 1,
usually reported as a percentage or per 1000.

```{webr}
# A survey of 2,400 adults found 312 with hypertension.
cases      <- 312
population <- 2400

prevalence <- cases / population
prevalence
round(prevalence * 100, 1)   # as a percentage
```

The answer is **0.13, or 13.0%**.

Prevalence describes a **snapshot**. It tells a health service how many people
need treatment today. It does not tell you how fast the disease is appearing,
because a case counted today may have started ten years ago.

::: {.callout-note}
## Point prevalence and period prevalence
**Point prevalence** is at one moment: "on 1 March, 312 of 2,400 adults had
hypertension."

**Period prevalence** is over a stretch: "during 2026, 410 of 2,400 adults had
hypertension at some point." It includes people who recovered in March and
people who fell ill in November, so it is always at least as large.

Say which one you mean. Papers that do not are a common cause of numbers that
will not reconcile.
:::

## Risk — what fraction fell ill over a period

Also called **cumulative incidence**. Now the denominator changes: only people
who *could* get the disease, counted at the *start*.

$$\text{Risk} = \frac{\text{new cases during the period}}{\text{people free of disease at the start}}$$

```{webr}
# 800 healthy factory workers followed for 2 years; 48 developed asthma.
new_cases <- 48
at_risk   <- 800

risk <- new_cases / at_risk
risk
```

The answer is **0.06, or 6% over two years**.

Risk is also a proportion between 0 and 1. Two things make it different from
prevalence:

1. Only **new** cases count. Someone who already had asthma is excluded from
   the numerator *and* from the denominator; they were never at risk.
2. **It is meaningless without a time period.** "A 6% risk" says nothing. "A 6%
   risk over two years" says something. Always attach the period.

## Rate — how fast, per unit of time at risk

Risk has a problem. It assumes everyone was followed for the whole period. In
any real study some people leave, some die of other things, some join late.
Counting them as if they were followed for two years overstates the denominator.

**Person-time** fixes this. Each person contributes exactly as much time as they
were actually observed and still at risk.

$$\text{Incidence rate} = \frac{\text{new cases}}{\text{total person-time at risk}}$$

```{webr}
# Five people, followed until the event or until they left the study.
#   A: 5.0 years, no event
#   B: 2.0 years, then the event
#   C: 5.0 years, no event
#   D: 1.5 years, then moved away
#   E: 3.0 years, then the event

person_years <- c(5.0, 2.0, 5.0, 1.5, 3.0)
events       <- c(0,   1,   0,   0,   1)

total_py     <- sum(person_years)
total_events <- sum(events)

total_py
total_events

# Rate per 100 person-years
round(total_events / total_py * 100, 1)
```

16.5 person-years, 2 events, so a rate of **12.1 per 100 person-years**.

3 things about a rate catch people out:

- **It has units.** Per person-year, per 1000 person-years. A rate without units
  is not a number you can interpret.
- **It is not a proportion.** It can exceed 1, and it can exceed 100%, because
  the denominator is time, not people. A rate of 150 per 100 person-years is
  perfectly possible.
- **Person-time stops when the person stops being at risk.** D contributed 1.5
  years, not 5. B contributed 2 years, not 5, because after the event they are
  no longer at risk of a first event.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Person-time assumes the rate is steady
Ten people followed for 1 year and one person followed for 10 years both give
10 person-years, and the formula treats them as equivalent. If the risk changes
with age, or with time since exposure, they are not equivalent at all. This is
why rates are usually calculated within age bands rather than over a whole
population at once.
:::

## Which measure answers which question

| The question | The measure | Denominator |
|---|---|---|
| How many patients need treatment today? | Prevalence | everyone, now |
| How likely is this person to fall ill in 5 years? | Risk | those at risk, at the start |
| How fast is disease appearing in this population? | Rate | person-time at risk |
| How much work will the clinic have? | Count | none |

## How the three relate

For a stable condition, prevalence rises both when disease appears more often
and when it lasts longer:

$$\text{Prevalence} \approx \text{Incidence rate} \times \text{Average duration}$$

```{webr}
# Incidence 10 new cases per 1000 person-years; average duration 4 years.
incidence_rate <- 10 / 1000   # per person-year
duration_years <- 4

round(incidence_rate * duration_years, 3)
```

About **0.04, or 4%** prevalent.

This explains something that often confuses people. **A treatment that keeps
patients alive without curing them raises prevalence.** Antiretroviral
therapy cut HIV incidence and HIV deaths, and the prevalence of people living
with HIV went up. Nothing went wrong; prevalence was never measuring what
people assumed.

::: {.callout-note}
## The approximation has conditions
It holds when incidence and duration have been roughly steady for long enough,
and when the disease is not common. In an outbreak, or for a condition
affecting a large share of the population, it breaks down. Use it to reason,
not to compute a number you will publish.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: prevalence"}
**Time:** 4 minutes

A house-to-house survey covered 1,850 people. 74 were found to have diabetes.

Compute the prevalence **per 1000 population**, rounded to 1 decimal place.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_prev
surveyed <- 1850
cases    <- 74

______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_prev
#| solution: true
surveyed <- 1850
cases    <- 74

round(cases / surveyed * 1000, 1)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_prev
#| check: true
# 74 / 1850 = 0.04 exactly, so 40.0 per 1000.
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 40))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — 40.0 per 1000, which is the same thing as 4%. Choose whichever unit makes your number easiest to read aloud.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.04))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the proportion. The question asked for it per 1000, so multiply by 1000.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 4))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the percentage. Per 1000 means multiplying by 1000, not by 100.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 25, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You divided the wrong way round. Cases go on top, population underneath.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Divide cases by surveyed, multiply by 1000, round to 1 place.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_prev"}
Prevalence is cases divided by population. "Per 1000" means multiplying that
proportion by 1000.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: risk"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

1,200 children were enrolled in a measles study. 90 of them **already had
immunity from past infection** and so could not get measles. Over the following
year, 111 of the rest developed measles.

Compute the one-year **risk**, as a proportion rounded to 3 decimal places.

Think carefully about the denominator.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_risk
enrolled      <- 1200
already_immune <- 90
new_cases     <- 111

______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_risk
#| solution: true
enrolled       <- 1200
already_immune <- 90
new_cases      <- 111

round(new_cases / (enrolled - already_immune), 3)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_risk
#| check: true
# At risk = 1200 - 90 = 1110.  111 / 1110 = 0.1 exactly.
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.1))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — 0.100, a 10% risk over one year. The 90 already-immune children belong in neither the numerator nor the denominator: they were never at risk.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 &&
           !is.na(.result) && abs(.result - 111/1200) < 0.001) {
  # 111/1200 is 0.0925, which R rounds to 0.092 at 3 places, not 0.093.
  # A tolerance band catches both spellings; an equality test on 0.093 would
  # make this branch unreachable.
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You used all 1,200 as the denominator. The 90 immune children could not get measles, so they were never at risk. Subtract them.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && .result > 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "A risk is a proportion and cannot exceed 1. Check which number you put on top.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right shape, wrong number. New cases divided by the number who were actually at risk at the start, rounded to 3.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "One number: new_cases divided by (enrolled - already_immune), rounded to 3 places.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_risk"}
Risk counts only people who could have got the disease. Ninety of the 1,200
could not.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 3: a rate from person-time"}
**Time:** 7 minutes

Six patients were followed after starting treatment. Their follow-up in years
and whether they relapsed:

| Patient | Years followed | Relapsed |
|---|---|---|
| A | 3.0 | no |
| B | 1.2 | yes |
| C | 3.0 | no |
| D | 0.8 | no (moved away) |
| E | 2.5 | yes |
| F | 1.5 | yes |

Compute the relapse rate **per 100 person-years**, rounded to 1 decimal place.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rate
years    <- c(3.0, 1.2, 3.0, 0.8, 2.5, 1.5)
relapsed <- c(0,   1,   0,   0,   1,   1)

______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rate
#| solution: true
years    <- c(3.0, 1.2, 3.0, 0.8, 2.5, 1.5)
relapsed <- c(0,   1,   0,   0,   1,   1)

round(sum(relapsed) / sum(years) * 100, 1)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_rate
#| check: true
# 3 relapses over 12.0 person-years = 25.0 per 100 person-years.
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 25))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — 3 relapses in 12.0 person-years, so 25.0 per 100 person-years. Note it is a rate, not a risk: D contributed only 0.8 years, not a whole person.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 50))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You divided by the number of people, not by person-time. That is the risk, 3 of 6. A rate divides by sum(years).")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.2, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You have the rate per person-year but have not multiplied by 100.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right shape, wrong number. sum(relapsed) on top, sum(years) underneath, times 100.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "One number: sum(relapsed) / sum(years) * 100, rounded to 1 place.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_rate"}
The numerator is how many relapses happened. The denominator is all the
follow-up time added together, not the number of patients.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 4: which measure? (on paper)"}
**Time:** 4 minutes. No code — answer these in your head, then check yourself
below.

For each question, name the measure you would use.

1. The state wants to know how many insulin pens to buy for next year.
2. A patient asks how likely she is to have a stroke in the next 10 years.
3. You want to know whether dengue is appearing faster this monsoon than last.
4. A hospital is planning how many dialysis chairs it needs.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answers"}
1. **Prevalence** (or a count). You need everyone currently needing insulin,
   however long ago they were diagnosed.
2. **Risk**, over 10 years. She is currently stroke-free, and the question has a
   time window built into it.
3. **Rate**. "Faster" is about speed, so the denominator has to be time.
4. **Prevalence** again. Existing patients on dialysis is exactly a snapshot.

If you found yourself wanting more information before answering, that instinct
is right, and it is most of the skill.
:::
:::

## What you should now be able to do

- Say why a count without a denominator cannot be compared between places.
- Compute a prevalence, and say whether it is point or period prevalence.
- Compute a risk, excluding from the denominator anyone who was not at risk.
- Compute an incidence rate from person-time, and state its units.
- Explain why a rate can exceed 100% and a risk cannot.
- Explain why a life-extending treatment raises prevalence.
